# Bastion

> One supervised MCP server process per profile, instead of one per editor. A signed macOS menu-bar
> app that runs each server once, keeps its credentials in the Keychain, and fronts it over loopback
> HTTP so several clients share one instance — with every tool call recorded.

macOS 26 or later, and macOS only. Shipping since 1.0.0 (August 2026): signed, notarized, and sold
direct at $14.99 (€14.99 in the EU, VAT included) for every 1.x release on every Mac you own. The
source is public and stays public; what is sold is the build. A 30-minute in-memory trial runs the
whole app, not a crippled version.

## The argument

- Every MCP client spawns its own copy of every stdio server. Three projects open in Claude Code is
  three `mcp-shopify` processes, three credential sets in three environments, no log, and no way to
  see what tool was called with what argument.
- The credentials are the sharp end. A `.mcp.json` holding a real secret in plaintext is readable by
  anything running as you and one careless `git add` from being published. Bastion holds them in the
  Keychain and hands them to a child at spawn; nothing in the app and nothing any client can call
  returns one once it is set.
- A **profile** is a named credential and configuration set — `prod/shopify`, `staging/shopify`,
  `rgis/keycloak`. It is the answer to the obvious objection to a shared gateway: one global instance
  is one identity, and one identity is unusable.
- The MCP handshake happens once, at spawn. Every client's `initialize` is answered from that one
  result, and each client's request ids are rewritten into the supervisor's own numbering and back,
  so two clients using id `1` at the same time cannot receive each other's answers.
- Write permission is per profile, not per process. `lab/unifi-network` with writes on beside
  `home/unifi-network` with writes off is expressible; a process boundary never made it so.

## Where clients point

```
http://127.0.0.1:8720/s/<profile>/<server>
```

Loopback only. Claude Code, VS Code, Cursor and ChatGPT & Codex reach that URL directly. Claude
Desktop, LM Studio and Windsurf are wired through `bastion-bridge`, a stdio shim that starts Bastion
on demand. Bastion writes those entries itself, one click per client, carries a revocable bearer
token in each one rather than a credential, and rewrites every wired client when a profile is added
or removed. Each extra Claude Code config directory (`~/.claude-<name>`) gets a row and a token of
its own. A workspace scopes profiles to folders: its profiles are written into Claude Code's
per-folder project blocks instead of the global list, so a session in one account's repository sees
only that account's servers. Workspaces are Claude Code only for now.

## What the record holds, and what it does not

- Recorded: the profile, the method, the tool name, the arguments it was called with, and — for a
  profile that opts in — the result and the outcome.
- Never recorded: credentials. Redaction happens before a row is written rather than filtered out
  afterwards.
- Never visible at all: what a server then does over the network or on disk. Bastion is the process
  holding the credential, not a proxy for the traffic. The page says so rather than implying
  otherwise.
- The log is a ring buffer in memory, cleared on quit. No argument and no result is written to disk
  unless you turn on the audit log in Settings › Activity, which appends hash-chained segments under
  Application Support. Nothing uploads it either way.
- Separately, and on by default: a usage rollup under Application Support. Per day, per profile and
  per tool — how many calls, how many bytes came back, how long they took, how many failed, how many
  times a server restarted. Counts only, with no arguments, no results, no resource paths and no
  identifiers, which is what lets it be on by default where the log is not. Kept ninety days, never
  uploaded, and Settings › Activity turns it off and deletes it. The Stats pane reads it.

## The five security rules

A loopback daemon holding every credential you own is a known shape of hole — CVE-2025-49596 was a
listener plus no CSRF protection, and a page you visited could reach it and execute code. All five
landed in the first commit rather than as a hardening pass:

1. Bind 127.0.0.1 explicitly. Never 0.0.0.0, and not configurable.
2. Validate Origin. The page-you-visited rule.
3. Validate Host. The anti-rebinding rule.
4. A per-client bearer token, minted at wiring time and kept in the Keychain.
5. Secrets never in a config file. The token goes in the client config; the credential stays in the
   Keychain.

Refusal order is load-bearing: a foreign Origin is refused before the token is even read.
`scripts/audit-listener.sh` asserts the listener binds loopback and nothing else, and `make audit`
runs it.

## Servers

Bastion ships with nothing installed. Thirty-four entries are in the catalog you install from. Twelve
are servers written here and run as child processes — App Store Connect, Reddit, X, UniFi Protect,
UniFi Network, Shopify, OVHcloud, Keycloak, npm, iOS Device, iOS Simulator and CloudKit.
Eleven more are child processes too, but published by somebody else: MongoDB, DBHub, Kubernetes,
Context7, Firecrawl, Exa, Tavily, Playwright, Supabase, Netlify and Apify — installed from npm and run
on your machine, with the supervision, the Keychain and the audit line around them but no review of the
code, which the app says on each one. The last eleven are https endpoints their own vendors operate:
Stripe, GitHub, Notion, Linear, Sentry, Atlassian, Figma, Vercel and three Cloudflare endpoints.
Anything else on npm can be added by package name, or by URL for a remote server.

Eighteen of the twenty-three children sit behind a write gate; Shopify, Context7, Firecrawl, Exa and
Tavily are read-only. The gate takes two shapes. Fourteen have an environment variable, and three of
those are inverted — MongoDB, DBHub and Kubernetes name a read-only switch rather than a write switch,
so Bastion sends the opposite value. The other four — Playwright, Supabase, Netlify and Apify — gate by
tool name instead, because their own read-only switch is a command-line flag and Bastion passes no
argv: the named tools are absent from tools/list with writes off. A remote server has no environment to
set either, so its writes are gated the same way. Code is fetched on demand into Bastion's own
directory and run with the embedded Node runtime.

`servers.json` at the repository root is the single source of truth for the catalog; the website's
table and the app's Swift catalog are both generated from it and CI fails on drift.

## Loading tools on demand

Off by default, per server or app-wide. Instead of the full listing, a client is served three
Bastion tools that search, describe and call the real ones, plus `bastion_call_write_tool` when the
server's writes are classified, so an editor's allowlist on the ordinary dispatcher cannot run a
write. Measured on `prod/appstore-connect`: 85 tools at 26.2k tokens become 0.4k, a 67× cut.
Clients that already load schemas on demand, Claude Code and Claude Desktop, are never fronted.

## Also in the app

- A Chat pane for trying a server's tools by hand.
- Bastion's own MCP server, so an agent can install servers, set credentials, manage profiles and
  workspaces and wire clients. Secrets are write-only there too.
- A provenance badge on the seventeen npm packages whose build attestation traces to the repository
  the catalog entry links.
- One press checks every npm-installed server for an update. Nothing checks on a timer.
- A server running on this Mac can be added by its literal `127.0.0.1` or `[::1]` URL over plain
  http.
- Launch at login, and a Stale entries card that removes client entries pointing at profiles that no
  longer exist.

## Protocol

Bastion serves the 2026-07-28 stateless revision to clients and speaks 2025-11-25 to its children,
translating between the two eras. Every catalog server is legacy today; the dialect layer is what
lets a client be modern anyway, and the day the last server flips is the day it can go. 24
conformance checks cover the translation.

## Privacy

The app opens exactly one network connection on its own: an update check, only after you turn
updates on. Installing a server, or pressing Check for Updates on one, reaches the npm registry, and
only on that press. No analytics, no telemetry, no crash reporter, no activation call. A licence key is an Ed25519
signature verified offline, so an installed copy does not know who bought it. Full inventory:
https://bastion.mgcrea.io/privacy
